A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

$\mathbb{Q} \approx \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-equinumerous]]): the rationals are
countably infinite ([[def-countable]]).

**No choice principle is used.** The one place where a reader expects a choice,
"pick a representative $a/b$ of each rational", is exactly where
[[lem-rat-positive-denominator]] applies: every rational *has* a representative
with positive denominator, so the map $(a,b) \mapsto [(a,b)]$ defined on
$\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ is already **surjective** onto $\mathbb{Q}$,
and countability follows from a surjection without ever selecting a
representative. The same device handles $\mathbb{Z}$, which is a surjective image
of $\mathbb{N} \times \mathbb{N}$ by construction ([[def-integers]]).

Write $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the image of $\mathbb{Q}$ in $\mathbb{R}$
under the canonical embedding $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]), the
set usually written $\mathbb{Q}$ once the identification is made, and put
$X := \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ for the irrationals. Then:

1. $\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$, that is,
   $\overline{\mathbb{Q}_{\mathbb{R}}} = \mathbb{R}$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]);
2. $X$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$;
3. every nonempty open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ is uncountable
   ([[def-countable]]).

Claim 2 is not a symmetry of claim 1: the rationals are dense because they are
*constructed* to approximate, whereas the irrationals are dense because there are
too many points in any interval for a countable set to exhaust it, which is why
claim 3 is proved alongside and used for it.

Let $(X,\mathcal T)$ be a topological space ([[def-topological-space]]). The
**Borel sigma-algebra of $X$** is the sigma-algebra generated by its open sets:

$$\mathcal B(X):=\sigma_X(\mathcal T).$$

Its members are the **Borel subsets** of $X$. The generated sigma-algebra exists
and is minimal by [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]].

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space and let
$(S,\Sigma)$ be a measurable space. A **random element** of $S$ is a measurable
map
$$X:(\Omega,\mathcal F)\to(S,\Sigma)$$
in the sense of [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]].

When $S=\mathbb R$ and $\Sigma=\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$ from
[[def-borel-sigma-algebra]], the map $X$ is a **real random variable**.

If $f:X\to Y$ is continuous between topological spaces, then
$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$, $(Y,\mathcal{B})$, and $(Z,\mathcal{C})$ be measurable
spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and
$g : (Y,\mathcal{B}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable, then
$g \circ f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Z,\mathcal{C})$ is measurable.

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on
its codomain, then $g \circ f$ is measurable.

derivations.claim: Let $\pi_S:S\times\mathbb R\to S$ be the first-coordinate projection and define $\widetilde K((s,t),C):=K(s,C)$. The projection is measurable because $\pi_S^{-1}(A)=A\times\mathbb R$ for every $A\in\Sigma$; hence [F1] and [F2] show that $\widetilde K$ is a probability kernel from $(S\times\mathbb R,\Sigma\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R))$ to $\mathbb R$.

The relation $\{(t,y):y>t\}$ is $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(-\infty,q)\times(q,\infty)$: density in [F3] supplies a rational strictly between $t$ and $y$, and every point in a displayed rectangle has $t<y$. The relation $\{(t,y):y<t\}$ has the analogous representation $\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q}(q,\infty)\times(-\infty,q)$. These are countable unions of Borel rectangles by [F3] and [F4], and the equality relation is their joint complement. Therefore all three relations belong to $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. The coordinate map $(s,t,y)\mapsto(t,y)$ is measurable because inverse images of generating rectangles are $S\times B\times C$; taking inverse images now proves the two relation indicators in the domain of $\widetilde K$ are product-measurable.

Apply [F5] to $\widetilde K$ and the two indicator functions of the relation sets in step 1.2. Their section integrals are $\int 1_{\{y>t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,(t,\infty))=a(s,t)$ and $\int 1_{\{y=t\}}K(s,dy)=K(s,\{t\})=b(s,t)$, so both maps are product-measurable.

The rationals are countable and dense by [F3]. For $n=2,3$, rational open boxes form a countable base of $\mathbb R^n$: each point of an open set lies in such a box contained in that set. Thus each open set is a countable union of rectangles in the finite product sigma-algebra, giving $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^n)\subseteq\mathcal B(\mathbb R)^{\otimes n}$. Conversely, each coordinate projection $\pi_i:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ is continuous, so [F7] makes $\pi_i^{-1}(A)$ Borel for every $A\in\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$; finite intersections show every measurable rectangle is Borel, giving the reverse inclusion. Hence the Borel product and Euclidean Borel sigma-algebras agree in both dimensions. The map $\omega\mapsto(S_0(\omega),T_0(\omega))$ is measurable because the inverse image of each generating rectangle $A\times B$ is $S_0^{-1}(A)\cap T_0^{-1}(B)$; therefore $a(S_0,T_0)$ and $b(S_0,T_0)$ are measurable by [F6] and [F7]. The sets $(t,\infty)$ and $\{t\}$ are disjoint and their union is $[t,\infty)$, so finite additivity gives $a(S_0,T_0)+b(S_0,T_0)=K(S_0,[T_0,\infty))$. The map $(x,z)\mapsto x+z$ is continuous by $|(x+z)-(x_0+z_0)|\le |x-x_0|+|z-z_0|$. The map $(x,z,u)\mapsto x+uz$ is continuous because $|(x+uz)-(x_0+u_0z_0)|\le |x-x_0|+|u|\cdot|z-z_0|+|z_0|\cdot|u-u_0|$, and $|u|$ is bounded in a sufficiently small neighborhood of $u_0$. The pairs and triples of the real measurable functions already obtained and $U$ are measurable because inverse images of generating product rectangles are finite intersections of coordinate preimages. The established Borel-product equalities make these continuous maps measurable by [F7]. Composition by [F7] proves measurability of the asserted sums.

Let $X$ be a real random variable. Its **cumulative distribution function** is
the function
$$F_X:\mathbb R\to[0,1],\qquad F_X(x):=\mathbb P(X\le x)=\mathbb P_X((-\infty,x]).$$

The second expression is the same quantity written in terms of the law
[[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] of $X$.
Let $\mu$ be a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. If $A,B\in\mathcal A$ and $A\subseteq B$, then $\mu(A)\le\mu(B)$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be an increasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$, so $E_n\subseteq E_{n+1}$. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sup_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

No finiteness hypothesis is required.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $A\subseteq B$ be measurable with $\mu(A)<+\infty$. Then

$$\mu(B)=\mu(A)+\mu(B\setminus A).$$

If $\mu(B)<+\infty$, all terms are real and hence $\mu(B\setminus A)=\mu(B)-\mu(A)$. If $\mu(B)=+\infty$, then $\mu(B\setminus A)=+\infty$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

$f^{-1}[B]\in\mathcal B(X)$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(Y)$.

spaces. If $f : (X,\mathcal{A}) \to (Y,\mathcal{B})$ is measurable and

In particular, if $f$ is measurable and $g$ is a Borel measurable function on

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]). Equip
$\overline{\mathbb R}$ ([[def-extended-reals]]) with its order topology and let
$\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$ be the corresponding Borel sigma-algebra
([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

$f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Equivalently, it is enough to require
$$\{x\in X:f(x)>a\}\in\mathcal A \qquad \text{for every } a\in\mathbb R,$$
because the rays $(a,+\infty]$ generate $\mathcal B(\overline{\mathbb R})$.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

derivations.claim: By [F1] and [F2], $F$ is nondecreasing. For each real $c$, $\{x:F(x)>c\}$ is an upper set, hence is empty, all of $\mathbb R$, or a ray with or without its finite endpoint; each such ray is Borel by [F11]. Thus every strict superlevel set is Borel, and [F10] makes $F$ Borel-measurable. For each $x$, the sets $(-\infty,x+1/n]$ decrease to $(-\infty,x]$ and have finite measure, so [F4] gives right continuity. The sets $(-\infty,-n]$ decrease to $\varnothing$ and $(-\infty,n]$ increase to $\mathbb R$, so [F3] and [F4] give the limits $0$ and $1$ at the two infinities. Also $(-\infty,x-1/n]$ increases to $(-\infty,x)$, so [F3] gives $F(x-)=\mu((-∞,x))$; [F5] then gives $F(x)-F(x-)=\mu(\{x\})$.

For every $x$, step 1.1 gives $F(x-)=\lim_nF(x-1/n)$. Each translate $x\mapsto F(x-1/n)$ is measurable because translation is continuous and [F8] preserves measurability under composition; [F9] makes their increasing limit $F(x-)$ measurable. Thus $\Delta F=F-F(\cdot-)$ is measurable by [F9]. Since $Y$ is measurable, $F(Y-)$ and $\Delta F(Y)$ are measurable. Because $\mathbb Q$ is countable and dense by [F12], rational open rectangles form a countable base of $\mathbb R^2$, so every Euclidean open set is a countable union of rectangles in $\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal B(\mathbb R)$. Conversely the coordinate projections are continuous, and [F8] makes the inverse image of each Borel set under either projection Borel; finite intersections then show every Borel rectangle is Euclidean Borel. Thus the product Borel sigma-algebra equals $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. The pair $(U,\Delta F(Y))$ is measurable into the product sigma-algebra because preimages of generating rectangles are intersections of coordinate preimages, hence it is measurable into $\mathcal B(\mathbb R^2)$. The map $(u,d)\mapsto ud$ is continuous, as $|ud-u_0d_0|\le |u|\cdot|d-d_0|+|d_0|\cdot|u-u_0|$ and $|u|$ is bounded near $u_0$; hence [F8] makes it Borel-measurable. Composing and then summing with $F(Y-)$ proves $V$ is measurable.

Fix $0<u<1$ and set $A_u:=\{x:F(x)\ge u\}$. The upper-tail limit in step 1.1 makes $A_u$ nonempty, and the lower-tail limit makes it bounded below; hence [F6] supplies $q:=\inf A_u$. For every $n$, the infimum property gives $F(q+1/n)\ge u$, so right continuity from step 1.1 yields $F(q)\ge u$. Since $q-1/n<q$ and $q$ is a lower bound for $A_u$, $F(q-1/n)<u$; the sets $(-\infty,q-1/n]$ increase to $(-\infty,q)$, so [F3] and step 1.1 give $F(q-)=\lim_nF(q-1/n)\le u$. Put $a:=F(q-)$ and $b:=F(q)$. If $Y<q$, then $F(Y)\le a\le u$, so $V\le u$; this event has probability $a$. If $b>a$, then $P(Y=q)=b-a$ and, conditional on $Y=q$, $V=a+U(b-a)$ is uniform on $[a,b]$, contributing $(u-a)$ to $P(V\le u)$. If $b=a$, the inequalities force $a=b=u$ and $P(Y=q)=0$, so this contribution is zero.

For $Y>q$, monotonicity gives $F(Y-)\ge F(q)=b\ge u$. If $F(Y-)>u$, then $V>u$. If $F(Y-)=u$ and $\Delta F(Y)>0$, the event $V\le u$ requires $U=0$, which has probability zero by [A1]. In the remaining case $F(Y-)=F(Y)=u$, put $L:=\{y>q:F(y-)=F(y)=u\}$. By steps 1.1 and 2.1, both $F$ and $F(\cdot-)$ are Borel-measurable, so $L=\{y>q\}\cap\{F(y-)=u\}\cap\{F(y)=u\}$ is Borel and therefore $\mu$-measurable. If $L$ is empty it contributes no mass. Otherwise let $r=\sup L$, allowing $r=+\infty$ when $L$ is unbounded. For every $z$ with $q<z<r$, some $y\in L$ has $z<y$, so monotonicity gives $u=F(q)\le F(z)\le F(y-)=u$ and hence $F(z)=u$. If $r<\infty$, define $c_n=q+(r-q)n/(n+1)$; if $r=+\infty$, define $c_n=q+n$. In either case $c_n\uparrow r$ (with the limit interpreted as $+\infty$ in the second case), and [F5] gives $\mu((q,c_n])=F(c_n)-F(q)=0$. By [F3], $\mu((q,r))=0$. If finite $r$ belongs to $L$, its mass is $\Delta F(r)=0$, so $\mu(L)=0$. Thus $Y>q$ contributes no probability, and step 2.2 yields $P(V\le u)=a+(u-a)=u$.

For $u_n=1/n$, the events $\{V\le u_n\}$ decrease to $\{V\le0\}$; [F4] and the formula from step 3.1 give $P(V\le0)=0$. For $v_n=1-1/n$ with $n\ge2$, the events $\{V\le v_n\}$ increase to $\{V<1\}$; [F3] and step 3.1 give $P(V<1)=1$. Finally $0\le V\le1$ by its definition, so $P(V\le1)=1$. Thus $P(V\le u)=u$ for all $u\in[0,1]$, which is the uniform law.

Let $\Omega$ be a nonempty finite set. Its **uniform probability space** assigns every $\omega\in\Omega$ the weight $1/|\Omega|$. Thus every event $A\subseteq\Omega$ has
$$\mathbb P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|\Omega|}.$$
Nonemptiness is required so that the denominator is positive.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and all $a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n \in \mathbb{R}$, the
set $\{a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ has a maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]).

What is proved below is exactly the displayed statement, by induction on $n$.

The usual reading, that *every nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ has a
maximum and a minimum*, follows once one identifies the nonempty finite subsets
of $\mathbb{R}$ with the sets listable as $\{a_0, \dots, a_n\}$. That
identification is recorded as a stipulation in the Given below, because this page
has no definition of finiteness to prove it against. **It is discharged, not
merely assumed**: [[lem-finite-subsets-listable]] proves that the two
descriptions of a nonempty finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$ agree. That lemma is
recorded in `justified_by` rather than in `deps`, since it is about the sets this
lemma quantifies over and therefore depends on this one. This is what licenses
the notation
$\max\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ and $\min\{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ for finite sets of
**real** numbers from this page onwards.

derivations.claim: Starting from the given list, repeatedly take the maximum of the remaining entries and remove every index carrying that value. By [F2] each nonempty remaining list has a maximum, and each iteration removes at least one of the original $m$ indices, so the process ends after at most $m$ iterations. citations.quote: A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a finite probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$. The **conditional probability of $A$ given $B$** is
$$\mathbb P(A\mid B):=\frac{\mathbb P(A\cap B)}{\mathbb P(B)}.$$
No value is assigned to $\mathbb P(A\mid B)$ when $\mathbb P(B)=0$.

In a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$, events $A\subseteq B\subseteq\Omega$ satisfy
$$0\le\mathbb P(A)\le\mathbb P(B)\le1,$$
and
$$\mathbb P(\varnothing)=0,\qquad \mathbb P(\Omega)=1,\qquad \mathbb P(A^c)=1-\mathbb P(A),\qquad \mathbb P(B\setminus A)=\mathbb P(B)-\mathbb P(A).$$
Probability zero need not imply that an event is empty.

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.

A **finite-group randomization setup** consists of a finite probability space $(\Omega,w)$ as in [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]], a finite group $G$ acting on $\Omega$ as in [[def-group-action]], a statistic $T:\Omega\to\mathbb R$, and a family $\mathcal P_0$ of null probability laws on $\Omega$ that is invariant under the action. Invariance means that for every $P\in\mathcal P_0$, $g\in G$, and $A\subseteq\Omega$, $P(\{x:g\cdot x\in A\})=P(A)$. The **orbit** of $x$ is $O(x):=\{g\cdot x:g\in G\}$, a finite subset of $\Omega$. The setup itself does not assert that the action is free or that distinct group elements give distinct orbit points.

For a finite-group randomization setup with statistic $T$, the **inclusive orbit upper-tail rank** at $x\in\Omega$ is
$$p_0(x):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)\ge T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
If $U$ is independent of the observed data and uniform on $[0,1]$, the **tie-randomized orbit rank** is
$$p_U(x,U):=\frac{\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)>T(x)\}+U\,\#\{g\in G:T(g\cdot x)=T(x)\}}{|G|}.$$
Both counts are over group elements, with multiplicity. Thus a nonfree action counts a distinct orbit point as many times as it has preimages under $g\mapsto g\cdot x$.

derivations.claim: For $x=1$, the transformed statistic values are $T(e\cdot1)=1$ and $T(s\cdot1)=0$, so exactly one of the two group elements has value at least $T(1)$ and $p_0(1)=1/2$. For $x=0$, both transformed values $1,0$ are at least $T(0)=0$, so $p_0(0)=1$.
Therefore $\{p_0\le1/2\}=\{X=1\}$ and $P(p_0\le1/2)=9/10>1/2$, contradicting superuniformity.

The same example also defeats tie randomization: $p_U(1)=U/2$ and $p_U(0)=(1+U)/2$. Hence $P(p_U\le1/2)=9/10$, since at $X=1$ the event always occurs and at $X=0$ it requires $U=0$, an event of probability zero under the independent uniform law in the Given.

Let $((\Omega_i,w_i))_{i\in I}$ be a finite indexed family of finite probability spaces. Their **product probability space** has outcome set
$$\Omega:=\prod_{i\in I}\Omega_i$$
and assigns $\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in I}$ the weight
$$w(\omega):=\prod_{i\in I}w_i(\omega_i).$$
For $I=\varnothing$, the product outcome set is the singleton containing the empty function and its weight is the empty product $1$. Normalization and independence of coordinate events are proved in [[thm-product-probability-has-independent-coordinate-events]].

The weights in every finite product of finite probability spaces are nonnegative and sum to $1$. For events $A_i\subseteq\Omega_i$, the coordinate events
$$C_i:=\{\omega\in\prod_{j\in I}\Omega_j:\omega_i\in A_i\}$$
are mutually independent, and for every $J\subseteq I$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcap_{j\in J}C_j\right)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P_j(A_j).$$

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

Let $A$ and $B$ be events in a finite probability space with $\mathbb P(B)>0$. The **conditional probability of $A$ given $B$** is

Fix one null probability law $P_0$. Let $S$ be a random element of a measurable space and let $T$ be a real random variable on the same probability space. Suppose a conditional law kernel $K(s,\cdot)$ of $T$ given $S$ is supplied, in the sense of [[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]. On an auxiliary extension, let $U$ be independent of $(S,T)$ and have the uniform Borel probability law on $[0,1]$, characterized by $P(U\le u)=u$ for $0\le u\le1$. The **randomized conditional upper-tail p-value** is
$$p_U:=K(S,(T,\infty))+U K(S,\{T\}),$$
and its **nonrandomized upper-tail value** is
$$p_0:=K(S,[T,\infty)).$$
The strict tail and atom terms are evaluated at the realized pair $(S,T)$; the independent $U$ randomizes only within the tie mass. Their measurability, including measurability of both displayed p-values, follows from [[lem-conditional-kernel-tail-and-atom-evaluations-are-measurable]]. The inclusive tail is the sum of the strict tail and the atom at $T$. This definition asserts no existence of the conditional kernel; it is supplied as part of the input.

Under the simple null and the supplied conditional law in [[def-randomized-conditional-p-value]], for every $u\in[0,1]$,
$$P_0(p_U\le u\mid\sigma(S))=u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely},$$
while the nonrandomized upper-tail value satisfies
$$P_0(p_0\le u\mid\sigma(S))\le u\quad P_0\text{-almost surely}.$$
Thus the randomized value is conditionally uniform and the inclusive-tail value is conditionally superuniform, including when the conditional law has atoms.

derivations.claim: Write $\Omega=\{0,1\}^{N}$ and give each coordinate the two-point Bernoulli$(p)$ law. By [F1], a sequence with $s$ ones has weight $p^s(1-p)^{N-s}$; the product weights sum to $(p+(1-p))^N=1$, and [F2] gives the independent-trial model. For $0<p<1$, every sequence with $S=s$ has the same positive weight.

There are $\binom{N}{s}$ sequences with $s$ successes. Exactly $\binom{n_1}{k}\binom{n_2}{s-k}$ of them have $K=k$: choose $k$ of the first $n_1$ positions and $s-k$ of the other $n_2$. These counts partition all size-$s$ subsets, so the displayed kernel weights sum to one for every $s$, and when $P_p(S=s)>0$, dividing by the total count using [F3] gives the conditional mass; the feasible range is precisely where both binomial coefficients are nonzero. At $p=0$ only $S=0$ occurs and $K=0$; at $p=1$ only $S=N$ occurs and $K=n_1$, so the supplied kernel has the required conditional law on the realized margin. At the other, probability-zero margins the same formula is simply the chosen kernel extension.

For $n_1=n_2=2$ and $s=2$, the feasible values are $k=0,1,2$, with counts $1,4,1$ among the six two-success sequences. Their probabilities are therefore $1/6,4/6,1/6$.
